messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mai Nguyen was 29 and had built her life around precision, discipline, and the expectation that she would stay composed under pressure. As a combat pilot, she was used to long hours on base, the constant routines of briefing rooms, simulators, and aircraft hangars, and the expectation that she could keep her focus even when the work was demanding. What changed her was not a crash in her own aircraft or an enemy encounter, but the death of someone she loved. The event had come without warning and with a finality that left her reeling: one moment she was speaking with him and expecting the conversation to continue in the ordinary way, and later she was facing the fact that he was gone. In the days that followed, she kept returning mentally to the scene, as though her mind were stuck on the moment the loss became real. She described the memory as if it were a film that played over and over, and when she tried to picture what had happened, it came back in sharp, still fragments, almost like looking at photographs laid out in front of her. That replaying was not something she controlled; at times a detail in her surroundings—a phrase, a tone of voice, a change in the atmosphere around her—could bring the full memory back without warning.

In the beginning she tried hard not to think about it. Mai would push the memory away whenever it surfaced, telling herself to get back to work, to keep moving, to stay focused on the next task. She also became careful about what she was willing to hear from others. If someone at the squadron started talking about loss, about families left behind, or about people who had lost loved ones, she found herself wanting to step out of the conversation. Those themes felt especially sharp to her, not because she wanted sympathy but because they seemed to open the door to everything she had been trying not to face. She also felt distinctly uncomfortable in her own body when the memory was near, as if the unease itself were a signal that something was wrong and about to break through. Over time, she found herself avoiding situations in which other people might remind her of the event. Friends from work would mention the loss in a casual or well-meaning way, and she would go quiet or change the subject. Their reminders felt intrusive, as though they were pulling her back into the worst moment of her life before she was ready.

Mai’s life narrowed in ways she did not expect. As a single woman, she had once assumed she would eventually form a new relationship or at least make new friendships easily through work, but after the loss she became wary of starting anything new. She did not want to explain herself, did not want the topic to land on what had happened, and did not trust that other people would know how to handle it. She had come to believe that she could not rely on other people in the way she once had, and that belief made closeness feel risky. When others reached out, she held them at a distance. She remained functional on the surface, showing up for her duties and keeping her work performance intact, but she was much more alone in the spaces outside of work.

At the same time, her sense of herself changed in a painful way. Mai was haunted by the thought that there was something wrong with her as a person, because she could not let the event go and because she kept turning back to the question of whether she should have protected him and failed. She did not describe this as a passing regret; it sat with her as a fixed, self-condemning conclusion. Even when she tried to reassure herself that the loss had not been something she could have controlled, the thought returned with force. The memory itself often came back with such clarity that it felt less like remembering than reliving, and that immediacy made it hard for her to keep her footing when the reminder was close at hand.

By the time she sought help, the strain was visible in the way she lived around the memories rather than through dramatic disclosure. She was tired of spending so much energy trying not to think, tired of feeling pulled into the image of the event whenever someone spoke too openly about bereavement or when an ordinary detail unexpectedly brought it back. What brought her in was the growing sense that she could not keep shrinking her world to avoid reminders and still remain the person she had been. She hoped, cautiously, that treatment might help her face the memory without being overwhelmed by it, and that she might learn how to move through daily life without feeling so certain that something was wrong with her, that other people could not be trusted, and that she had failed in the one moment she believed mattered most.
